refined_brief: Source-grounded 4:3 black/white abstracts with framed subfigures, appropriate quantitative plots, explained terminology, consistent spacing and right-aligned source credits.
central_argument: The financially strongest option need not minimize emissions; grid-electrolysis hydrogen depends on transition timing and the electricity pathway.
source_evidence: Published Table 2: nonlinear model, Mid (middle) technology, 10-year vehicle life, Australian government baseline grid. Transition-year scenarios are 2025, 2030 and 2035. Lifetime emissions are tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per vehicle; financial values are return on investment percentages relative to matched diesel. The diesel emissions reference is 2173 tonnes. In these scenarios grid-electrolysis hydrogen drops below diesel emissions by 2030 (1239 tonnes) but remains financially negative (-254 percent); it becomes positive by 2035 (389 percent). Battery emissions fall to 298 tonnes, while gray-hydrogen fuel cells reach 3209 percent return. Values are transcribed in transition-results.csv. The five mechanisms follow the model methods. Scenario factors are five powertrains, three technology paths (constant/middle/advanced), one baseline grid, three vehicle lives (5/10/15 years), three transition years, and two model modes (linear/nonlinear), totaling 270. The 25-year study horizon differs from vehicle life.
limitations: A reported-value replot, not a new simulation or execution of the recovered synthetic-data demo. Connected points compare modeled adoption-year scenarios, not longitudinal observations. One deterministic value per scenario; no replicate or uncertainty interpretation. The paper calls grid-electrolysis hydrogen green hydrogen; the figure names the electricity source explicitly. Table 2 values are used consistently rather than reconciling inconsistent prose by inventing values.
